query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a liquid-phase precursor processing route with a subsequent low‐temperature heat treatment around 1800 °C will enable the synthesis of single-phase ZrB2 ceramic with ultrafine, uniformly distributed grains, thereby lowering the conventional preparation temperature (above 2300 °C) and reducing microporosity that leads to failures during prolonged liquid plating exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous liquid precursor composed of zirconium and boron (and any necessary complexing agents) that transforms into a reactive intermediate (metal oxides and amorphous boron compounds) upon initial low-temperature pyrolysis.
generation.intervention: Use a liquid precursor processing route with controlled low‐temperature heat treatment (e.g., ramping to ~1800 °C) instead of the conventional high-temperature (>2300 °C) sintering.
generation.conditions: Preparation under an inert (or reducing) atmosphere with a controlled ramp rate up to ~1800 °C; subsequent densification and consolidation steps; service conditions include prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath where chemical and thermal stability is critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ultrafine, uniformly distributed ZrB2 grains with reduced pore volume and enhanced interparticle bonding resulting from the molecular-level mixing in the liquid precursor method.
generation.mechanism: The liquid precursor route promotes intimate mixing of Zr and B at the molecular scale, leading to earlier formation of reactive intermediates that require a lower thermal activation energy for forming the single-phase ZrB2. This results in a denser, more uniform microstructure with fewer processing-induced defects (e.g., holes) that typically arise during prolonged high-temperature treatments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventionally prepared ZrB2 (sintered above 2300 °C), the ceramic prepared via the liquid precursor method at ~1800 °C will exhibit lower porosity, finer and more uniform grain structure, and therefore enhanced structural integrity and resistance to degradation when exposed to prolonged liquid plating environments.
generation.baseline: Conventionally synthesized single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, produced by high-temperature sintering (>2300 °C), which typically displays higher porosity and structural imperfections that contribute to the formation of holes and subsequent component failure during service.
generation.boundary: Preparation temperatures up to approximately 1800 °C using the liquid precursor method; service conditions involve extended exposure to a liquid plating bath where thermal and chemical robustness is required.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how effectively the enhanced nano-scale homogeneity achieved through the liquid precursor method will translate into macroscopic mechanical integrity after full-scale sintering and long-term plating exposure. Variability in the precursor chemistry and processing parameters may also affect the final phase purity and density.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 ceramics: one via the conventional high-temperature method (>2300 °C) and one via the liquid precursor method with heat treatment at ~1800 °C. Characterize both sets for phase purity, microstructure, density, and porosity. Subject both samples to identical long-duration exposure tests in a liquid plating bath. Compare the evolution of microstructural features and mechanical properties (e.g., flexural strength, fracture toughness) before and after plating exposure.
measurements: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) for microstructural and compositional analysis
Density and porosity measurements (e.g., Archimedes method)
Mechanical testing (flexural strength, fracture toughness) before and after plating exposure
Long-duration liquid plating bath immersion tests with periodic examination for hole formation or structural degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the liquid precursor-processed ceramic does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in density (i.e., lower porosity), microstructural uniformity, and mechanical integrity after plating exposure compared to the conventional ceramic, or if it fails prematurely under plating conditions, then the hypothesis that the intervention lowers preparation temperature and improves service performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractA nano-dual-phase powder with ultra-fine grain size was synthesized by the liquid precursor method at 1200 °C. A series of single-phase high-entropy ceramic powders ((Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2) with high purity (C content less than 0.9 wt% and O content less than 0.7 wt%) and ultrafine (average grain sizes of 340–570 nm) were successfully synthesized at 1800 °C. The sample of (TiZrHfNbTa)B2 exhibited a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, and the metal elements were uniformly distributed at the nanoscale, microscale, and macroscale. This method did not apply to the preparation of all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for the formation of single-phase high-entropy borides when the size difference factor exceeded 3.9%. The present work provides a guide for the development of ceramic-based composites through precursor impregnation pyrolysis.Keywords: liquid-phase precursor method, high-entropy diboride powders, solid solutions, microstructure, pyrolysis mechanism

Hence, there is an urgent need to synthesize high-purity, high-entropy metal diboride powders to further promote the development of high-entropy boride ceramics. Yan Zhang et al. [], using B, ZrO2, HfO2, Ta2O5, Nb2O5, and TiO2 powders as raw materials, produced a nano-dual-phase powder by molten salt-assisted borothermal reductions at 1100 ◦C. The as-synthesised powder has a specific surface area of 22.971 m2/g, according to the BET measurement result, implying good sinterability. Dong Zhijun et al. [] used precursor polyboron nitride (PBN) as the boron source and an organic precursor of HfC to synthesize HfB2 ceramic powders with particle sizes of about 200 nm through a liquid-phase route at 1500 °C. (Hf, Nb, Cr, Ta, Mo)B2 ceramic powder with an average particle size of 62.09 nm was obtained by the sol-gel method at a relatively low temperature of 1650 °C. Molten salt and sol-gel methods contribute to the synthesis of low-temperature fine grains, but the processability of these methods can be inferior. cited_evidence.text: Based on the above analysis, we hypothesize the decomposition mechanism of the (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2 liquid precursor as depicted in Figure 11. During the heat treatment process below 800 °C, the liquid precursor primarily undergoes an organic-to-inorganic transformation, leading to the formation of various metal oxide solid solutions and amorphous carbon and boron oxides. When the decomposition temperature falls within the range of 1000 °C to 1400 °C, the main process involves a carbon-boron thermal reduction reaction, resulting in a two-phase structure primarily composed of (Zr, Hf)B2 and (Ti, Nb, Ta)B2. As the decomposition temperature increases from 1600 °C to 1800 °C, the process primarily entails phase solid solution, ultimately culminating in the formation of the hexagonal (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2 single-phase solid solution.

chosen.approach: Liquid precursor processing route with low‐temperature heat treatment
